clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive defect in tyrosine catabolism caused by deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, allowing homogentisic acid to accumulate
The classic and often earliest sign is urine that turns dark brown or black on standing or on alkalinisation, sometimes noticed as dark-staining nappies in infancy
Ochronosis, the bluish-black pigmentation of connective tissue, becomes apparent in adulthood, notably in the ear cartilage and the sclerae
A severe, early-onset degenerative arthropathy, particularly of the spine and large joints, is the major cause of morbidity
Deposition of ochronotic pigment can also affect heart valves (aortic stenosis and valve calcification), cause pigmented renal and prostate stones, and stiffen tendons
Diagnosis is confirmed by markedly elevated urinary homogentisic acid, and the disorder is usually benign in childhood with complications emerging over decades
Management is largely symptomatic with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint care; nitisinone, which reduces homogentisic acid production, is being used to slow disease progression
It is one of the original inborn errors of metabolism described by Garrod but is not a routine newborn screening target, being clinically mild early in life
reference.pathophysiology: Alkaptonuria results from deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, an enzyme in the pathway that degrades tyrosine and phenylalanine. The block causes homogentisic acid to accumulate and be excreted in large amounts in urine, where it oxidises and polymerises to a dark pigment, explaining the darkening of urine. Over years, oxidised homogentisic acid deposits as ochronotic pigment in collagen-rich connective tissues, particularly cartilage, tendons, sclerae and heart valves. This pigment makes cartilage brittle and provokes a progressive degenerative arthropathy, and its deposition in other tissues underlies the cardiac, renal and cutaneous manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of dark urine (haematuria, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, porphyria, drug effects)
Osteoarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis for the arthropathy
Exogenous ochronosis (e.g. from hydroquinone or phenol exposure)
Degenerative disc and joint disease of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Simple test of urine darkening on standing or alkalinisation
Molecular testing of the HGD gene
Imaging of the spine and large joints for ochronotic arthropathy and disc calcification
Echocardiography for valvular involvement in adults
Assessment for renal and prostate stones where indicated
redFlags: Symptomatic aortic valve stenosis or significant valve calcification requiring cardiac assessment
Severe, disabling spinal or large-joint arthropathy
Obstructing pigmented renal or prostatic stones
Rapid functional decline from progressive joint destruction in adulthood
reference.prognosis: Alkaptonuria is compatible with a normal lifespan and is largely asymptomatic in childhood, but progressive ochronotic arthropathy and, less often, cardiac and renal complications cause substantial disability in later adult life; disease-modifying therapy aims to slow this progression.
pitfalls: Dismissing dark urine as a benign curiosity and missing the underlying diagnosis
Attributing the arthropathy to ordinary osteoarthritis without recognising ochronosis
Overlooking cardiac valve and renal stone complications during long-term follow-up
Confusing endogenous ochronosis with exogenous pigmentation from topical or occupational exposure
management: Nitisinone lowers homogentisic acid production by inhibiting the upstream enzyme and is the disease-modifying therapy that slows ochronosis
Consider dietary restriction of phenylalanine and tyrosine to limit substrate, particularly alongside nitisinone, and monitor for tyrosinaemia and keratopathy
Manage the ochronotic arthropathy with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint replacement for advanced large-joint and spinal disease
Monitor for cardiac valve involvement with echocardiography and refer for aortic valve intervention when significant
Screen for and manage pigmented renal and prostatic stones
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across metabolic medicine, rheumatology, orthopaedics and cardiology
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder
